_comment: Curated concept graph (plan §36.2, Tier 3). Each concept names the concepts it presupposes and the generated notes (by stem) that define it: far = FAR section or part index stems, aim = AIM paragraph/section stems, pcg = glossary term stems, see_also = any vault stem including curated notes. Descriptions are the curator's own words — study aids, never regulatory text. Rebuild with `far-aim build-vault`; unresolved references, cycles and title collisions fail the build.

concepts.title: How Title 14 Is Organized
concepts.description: The FARs are Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations, divided into parts (Part 61 for pilots, Part 91 for operating rules); a citation such as § 91.155 names one section within a part.

concepts.title: Regulatory Definitions
concepts.description: Part 1 defines the words the rest of Title 14 uses (night, category, class, flight time, cross-country); Part 61 adds its own definitions for pilot certification.

concepts.title: Pilot in Command Authority
concepts.description: The pilot in command is directly responsible for, and the final authority over, the operation of the aircraft, and may deviate from the rules to the extent an in-flight emergency requires.

concepts.title: Careless and Reckless Flying
concepts.description: Independent of every specific rule, no one may operate an aircraft carelessly or recklessly, interfere with a crewmember, or drop objects that endanger people or property.

concepts.title: Pilot Certificates and Ratings
concepts.description: Who needs a pilot certificate, what it must be accompanied by, how long it lasts, and the category, class and type ratings placed on it.

concepts.title: Medical Certification
concepts.description: Which operations require which class of medical certificate, how long each class lasts, when BasicMed can substitute, and the duty not to fly with a known disqualifying condition.

concepts.title: Alcohol and Drugs
concepts.description: The eight-hour and 0.04 percent rules for crewmembers, the refusal-to-test consequences, and the certificate actions that follow drug and alcohol offenses.

concepts.title: Student Pilot Privileges
concepts.description: What a student pilot must have before soloing, the endorsements that gate solo and solo cross-country flight, and the operations a student may never conduct.

concepts.title: Private Pilot Eligibility and Privileges
concepts.description: The age, knowledge, training and aeronautical-experience requirements for a private pilot certificate, and the limits on carrying passengers or sharing costs once it is held.

concepts.title: Additional Aircraft Endorsements
concepts.description: Aircraft that need a one-time logbook endorsement beyond the category and class rating: complex, high-performance, pressurized, and tailwheel airplanes, plus type ratings for large and turbojet aircraft.

concepts.title: Recent Flight Experience
concepts.description: The flight review every 24 calendar months and the three takeoffs and landings (to a full stop at night) within 90 days before carrying passengers.

concepts.title: Logbooks and Required Pilot Documents
concepts.description: Which flights must be logged and how, which documents a pilot must carry, and how logged time proves recent experience and eligibility.

concepts.title: Cross-Country Time
concepts.description: Cross-country time means different things for different certificates; the tiers in § 61.1 decide which flights count toward each experience requirement.

concepts.title: Airworthiness Responsibility
concepts.description: The pilot in command decides whether the aircraft is in condition for safe flight, and the owner or operator keeps it airworthy through required inspections and maintenance records.

concepts.title: Aircraft Documents and Flight Manual
concepts.description: The airworthiness certificate and registration that must be aboard, and the operating limitations, flight manual and placards the aircraft must be flown within.

concepts.title: Required VFR Equipment
concepts.description: The instruments and equipment required for day and night VFR flight, the emergency locator transmitter, and what to do when installed equipment is inoperative.

concepts.title: Transponders and ADS-B Out
concepts.description: Where a transponder and ADS-B Out are required, how to operate them, and the codes and phraseology that go with them.

concepts.title: Airspace Classification
concepts.description: The classes of controlled and uncontrolled airspace (A through G), how they nest and overlap, and where each is charted.

concepts.title: Operating in Controlled Airspace
concepts.description: The entry, communication, equipment and speed rules for Class B, C, D and E airspace, and what changes at an airport in Class G.

concepts.title: Special Use and Other Airspace
concepts.description: Prohibited, restricted, warning and alert areas, military operations areas, military training routes, terminal radar service areas, and temporary flight restrictions.

concepts.title: National Security Airspace and ADIZ
concepts.description: Air defense identification zones, the Washington DC special flight rules area, national security areas, and the interception procedures every pilot must recognize.

concepts.title: VFR Visibility and Cloud Clearance
concepts.description: The flight visibility and distance-from-cloud minimums for VFR flight in each airspace class, day and night, and the surface-area rule for taking off, landing or entering the pattern.

concepts.title: Special VFR
concepts.description: Operating below basic VFR minimums within a surface area under an ATC clearance: the visibility floor, the clear-of-clouds rule, and the night and instrument-rating conditions.

concepts.title: Minimum Safe and VFR Cruising Altitudes
concepts.description: The minimum altitudes over congested and other areas, the east/west hemispheric cruising altitudes above 3,000 feet AGL, and the altimeter setting to fly them by.

concepts.title: Right-of-Way Rules
concepts.description: Who gives way when aircraft converge, approach head-on, overtake or land, the see-and-avoid duty in VFR conditions, and the speed limits below 10,000 feet and in airspace surface areas.

concepts.title: Night Operations
concepts.description: How night is defined for equipment, logging and recent experience, the lighting rules, and the vision and illusion effects that make night flying different.

concepts.title: Aviation Weather Services
concepts.description: Where preflight and in-flight weather comes from, the forecast and observation products (TAF, METAR, GFA), in-flight advisories, and pilot weather reports.

concepts.title: Thunderstorms Icing and Wind Shear
concepts.description: The weather a VFR pilot must recognize and avoid: thunderstorms, airframe icing, microbursts and wind shear, and how to report them.

concepts.title: ATC Communications
concepts.description: Radio technique, contact procedure, call signs, the phonetic alphabet, and how altitudes, directions, speeds and time are spoken on the air.

concepts.title: ATC Facilities and Services for VFR Aircraft
concepts.description: What control towers, approach control, centers and flight service stations do for a VFR pilot, including flight following, radar traffic information and safety alerts.

concepts.title: ATC Clearances and Instructions
concepts.description: What a clearance is, the pilot's duty to follow it or ask for an amended one, and when deviating from an instruction is permitted.

concepts.title: Airport Markings Signs and Lighting
concepts.description: Runway and taxiway markings, holding position markings, the sign system, and the runway and approach lighting a pilot must read on the ground and from the air.

concepts.title: Towered and Non-Towered Airports
concepts.description: Operating at airports with and without an operating control tower: traffic advisory practices, visual indicators, light signals, runway selection and communications.

concepts.title: Traffic Pattern Procedures
concepts.description: The standard left-hand pattern and its legs, pattern altitudes, entry and departure, and the maneuvers that are unexpected in the pattern.

concepts.title: Taxiing and Runway Incursion Avoidance
concepts.description: Taxi clearances and read-backs, hold-short lines, land-and-hold-short operations, exiting the runway, and taxiing in low visibility.

concepts.title: Wake Turbulence Avoidance
concepts.description: How wingtip vortices form and behave, where they are most dangerous, and the avoidance procedures and separation minima that follow.

concepts.title: Preflight Action and VFR Fuel
concepts.description: The information a pilot in command must be familiar with before any flight, and the day and night VFR fuel reserves.

concepts.title: NOTAMs
concepts.description: The notice to airmen system: what NOTAMs cover, how they are classified, and where a pilot obtains them before flight.

concepts.title: VFR Flight Plans
concepts.description: Filing, activating, changing and closing a VFR flight plan with flight service, and what happens when one is left open.

concepts.title: Passengers and Safety Belts
concepts.description: The safety-belt and child-restraint rules, the required passenger briefing, and the crew-at-station and carriage-for-hire limits a private pilot flies under.

concepts.title: Aeromedical Factors
concepts.description: Hypoxia, hyperventilation, carbon monoxide, ear and sinus blocks, spatial disorientation and vision, and the supplemental oxygen rules that address altitude.

concepts.title: Collision Avoidance
concepts.description: Scanning technique, the judgment aspects of collision avoidance, and the traffic information services that supplement see-and-avoid.

concepts.title: VFR Flight Hazards
concepts.description: Bird activity, obstructions, mountain flying, VFR in congested areas, unmanned aircraft and laser illumination: the hazards the AIM singles out for VFR pilots.

concepts.title: Emergencies and Deviations
concepts.description: Declaring distress or urgency, the emergency authority to deviate, transponder emergency codes, radar assistance, and what to do after a two-way radio failure.

concepts.title: Emergency Locator Transmitters and Search and Rescue
concepts.description: ELT requirements and testing, how a search is triggered when a flight plan is not closed, and what the search-and-rescue system expects of pilots.

concepts.title: Accident and Incident Reporting
concepts.description: The NTSB notification and reporting duties after an accident or serious incident, near-midair collision reports, and the Aviation Safety Reporting Program.
